newsitem.title: GERMANY: Israel's envoy says he has warmed to Germany.
newsitem.headline: Israel's envoy says he has warmed to Germany.

text.p: Israel's ambassador to Germany, Avi Primor, who once thought he would never have contact with the country after the horrors of Nazism, on Wednesday said much had changed.

"After World War Two... I was sure I would never come into contact with Germany or Germans and I would never buy German goods. But today our son Daniel is the first child of an Israeli diplomat to go to a German school," Primor told guests at the launch of his new book on his experience in Bonn.
"With the exception of Germany", published in German and due to be translated into Hebrew, describes the change in Primor's -- and Israel's -- relationship with Germany.

Primor, who took up the post of ambassador in 1993, said the most important development prompting him to change his perception of Germany had been its recognition of the past and the crimes committed during the Nazi era.
"To quote a 16th century rabbi: 'In remembrance one finds the solution,'" Primor said.

German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel praised Primor's book and said it gave an insight into his personal experiences and thoughts and drew a clear picture of history and the post-war improvement of relations between Israel and Germany.
"Your life, ambassador, reflects this approach in an exemplary manner," Kinkel said at the launch.
Primor, whose mother and grandfather escaped from Nazi Germany to Israel, said Israelis as well as Germans had tried to forget the past and urged his compatriots to do more to understand Germany.
"We tried to repress the past too. Perhaps that was because of the pain, but it meant we didn't build bridges."
Both Kinkel and Primor said Germany was now Israel's second most important partner after the United States.

Kinkel stressed that Germany was at Israel's side when it came to securing its existance and would continue to do all it could, along with its European Union partners, to help the Middle East peace process.

"The peace process must continue without any further pre-conditions. Negotiations must be started again immediately. The contractual obligations which have already been reached must be complied with in spirit and to the letter," he said.
Primor said there was no alternative to the peace process and acknowledged Germany's role in supporting it. "In terms of the peace process we have a joint future," he said.
